warmup.q: A program that flags card payments as possible fraud never sees a customer's ethnicity or neighbourhood. It looks at the device, how quickly payments come, the amount, and a postcode risk score learned from past fraud investigations. Can it still treat two groups of customers differently?
options: No: without the group, it has nothing to tell them apart by
Only if someone mislabelled the past examples it learned from, on purpose
Yes: the postcode score can carry the history of who was investigated, and stand in for the group
Only if one group really commits more fraud
warmup.why: If investigators used to check some neighbourhoods far more often, more fraud was recorded in those postcodes, and a score learned from the records flags their residents more, whatever they actually do. In this lesson's demo, both groups commit fraud at the same 1% rate and the program never sees the group. Yet honest customers in one group are flagged by mistake 8.3% of the time, against 2.3% in the other. The first option is the trap: removing a column doesn't remove what other inputs know.

sections.h: A program that decides about people repeats the past, and someone must answer for it
sections.html:
In 2016 ProPublica, an American newsroom, followed more than 7,000 people arrested in Broward County, Florida. Each had been scored by COMPAS, a tool that predicts whether someone will commit another crime. Among those who did not commit another crime within two years, 44.9% of Black defendants had been labelled higher risk, against 23.5% of white defendants.

In 2019 Obermeyer and colleagues looked at a program from Optum, a US health company, that picked patients for extra care. It predicted each patient's future health costs, as a stand-in for how much care they needed. Less money is spent on Black patients with the same illnesses, so the program scored them as healthier than they were. Predicting need instead of cost would have raised the share of Black patients picked for extra help from 17.7% to 46.5%.

Both programs are models: programs that learn a rule from past examples, called training data, and apply it to new cases. The mechanism is the same in both. A model learns from records of past decisions and past spending, not from the truth. And a proxy, an input that stands in for something else (a postcode, a cost, an address), carries the group into the model after the group's column was removed.

This lesson's demo builds a fraud model, a program that flags payments as possible fraud, that never sees the group. Both groups commit fraud at the same rate, but one group's postcodes were investigated more in the past. Honest customers in that group are flagged by mistake 8.3% of the time, against 2.3% in the other. A flag on an honest payment is called a false positive. You only see the gap if you measure error rates for each group. That means knowing each customer's group for the check, which is itself sensitive data that needs care.

Predictions also change the data the next model learns from. Flag more payments in one area, investigate more there, record more fraud there, and the postcode score rises again. That's a feedback loop: the model's decisions write its own next lesson.

Then comes accountability: who answers when the system is wrong? On 21 August 2026 the Dutch data protection authority, the Netherlands' regulator for personal data, fined Uber €824,990,000. That's the second-largest fine so far under the GDPR, the EU's main law on personal data. From 2018 to 2022, Uber had shut drivers out of their accounts by fully automated decisions, on suspected fraud or low ratings. No person reviewed them, and drivers weren't told. Uber is appealing.

Article 22 of the GDPR gives people the right not to be subject to decisions made solely by software that significantly affect them. The exceptions still need safeguards, such as a person who can review the decision. For a data system, that means three things. Keep a record of each decision with its inputs, model version and reasons. Staff a review queue with people who can overturn it. And give the person a way to contest it and correct the data it used.

Sellers of such models can be sued too. In May 2025, in Mobley v. Workday, a US court let age-discrimination claims against the seller of an AI tool that screens job applicants go ahead, as one lawsuit on behalf of many people. No court had decided whether the claims were true by November 2026.

A decision made by software still needs someone who answers for it. Record it, and let a person overturn it.

Every one of these decisions was built from records about people. Next, we'll ask whether those records should exist at all.

try.title: A model that never sees the group
steps: From the labs folder, run the demo below. It is a made-up example built to show one mechanism: 20,000 card payments, 30% from neighbourhood B, real fraud at 1% in both groups, and a model that flags the riskiest 5%.

Model A adds a postcode risk score to a behaviour score. The postcode score was learned from past investigations that checked B's postcodes far more often. Model B uses behaviour only. Predict: which model treats honest customers in A and B differently, and does dropping the postcode cost much fraud caught?
Look at caught for both models. What would you need to know about each payment to even notice the difference in false alarms?

code.title: FairnessDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: val postcode = (if (b) 0.6 else 0.3) + 0.1 * gauss() // reflects past investigations, not fraud val behaviour = (if (fraud) 1.5 else 0.0) + 0.5 * gauss() // device, velocity, amount: real signal report("model A: postcode risk + behaviour (no group column)", payments) { it.postcodeRisk + it.behaviour } report("model B: behaviour only", payments) { it.behaviour }

try.expect:
-- model A: postcode risk + behaviour (no group column)
   group  payments  fraud  caught  false alarms  false-positive rate
   A         14068    149     127           325                 2.3%
   B          5932     62      59           489                 8.3%
-- model B: behaviour only
   group  payments  fraud  caught  false alarms  false-positive rate
   A         14068    149     133           560                 4.0%
   B          5932     62      55           252                 4.3%

Model A never reads the group, yet an honest customer in B is more than three times as likely to have a payment blocked. Model B treats the two groups about the same, and it catches 188 frauds against model A's 186. To see any of this you need the group of each payment when you check the model, and that's the uncomfortable part: measuring fairness needs the sensitive data you were trying not to use. The numbers come from a simulation, not a study; the mechanism is the one ProPublica and Obermeyer found.

sections.h: Privacy is the right to decide, and personal data is a risk to keep small
sections.html:
A payments company sees every purchase: the pharmacy, the clinic, the bar, the betting site, the donation. Card data can reveal someone's health, religion, sexuality and debts without anyone ever typing those words. When a system stores what you entered for your own purpose, you are its customer. When it also records your behaviour on the side and uses it for someone else (advertising, scoring, selling it on), you become the subject of surveillance.

Privacy isn't the same as secrecy. It's the right to decide what to reveal, to whom, and for what. Tracking moves that decision from the person to whoever holds the data. A privacy setting in an app usually controls what other users can see, and says little about what the company does with the data itself.

Consent, asking people first, is the obvious answer, and it's weaker than it looks. Under the GDPR, consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and as easy to withdraw as to give, so a box that comes ticked doesn't count. It's also only one of six legal grounds for using personal data. Fraud checks, for example, usually rest on the company's legitimate interests or a legal duty instead. In practice, few people can know what a dataset will be joined with later. Data about one person reveals others, such as contacts and relatives. And saying no to a service everyone else uses has a real cost.

Data is also a liability, a risk that can cost money. 23andMe, a company that read people's DNA from saliva samples, held the genetic data of more than 13 million customers. In 2023 a credential-stuffing attack, logging in with passwords leaked from other sites, exposed customers' data. The UK's data regulator, the Information Commissioner, later fined the company £2.31 million. The company filed for bankruptcy in March 2025. A court approved the sale of its assets, the genetic data included, to TTAM Research Institute for $305 million. 27 US states and the District of Columbia sued over consent. People who mailed a saliva sample to one company found their DNA sold as an asset of a bankrupt one. Data outlives the company that collected it, its promises and its owners.

So collect less. The GDPR's principles say it plainly. Purpose limitation: use data only for the purposes it was collected for. Data minimization: collect only what those purposes need. Storage limitation: keep it no longer than they need. Data you don't hold can't leak, can't be demanded by a court and can't be sold in a bankruptcy. In practice, keep only totals when a feature needs only totals. Give every dataset a retention period, a time after which it is deleted. And pseudonymize where analysis doesn't need to know who someone is: replace names and card numbers with a stand-in key. A pseudonymized record is still personal data, because someone can still link the key back to the person.

Data you don't keep can't hurt anyone. Collect less, and give everything an end date.

Collecting less shrinks the problem. Next, we'll read what the law asks of systems.

try.title: Keep only what one feature needs
steps: A new feature shows each customer their monthly spending by category (groceries, travel, eating out). The team proposes to read the full payment event: card number, cardholder name, email, IP address, device fingerprint, GPS location, shop ID, the shop's category code, amount, currency, time and the basket's items.
Decide which fields the feature needs, which it can do without, and what you would store instead of the raw events.
Write down the retention period you'd give the stored data.
try.expect: It needs a customer key (a stand-in ID, not the card number or the email), the shop's category code, the amount, the currency and the month. It doesn't need the card number, name, email, IP address, device fingerprint, location, shop ID or basket items. Store a running total per (customer key, month, category) instead of copies of the events: a few hundred bytes per customer per month instead of every payment. The totals are still personal data, since they are tied to a customer key. So give them a retention period that matches the feature (say 13 months, to show a year against the year before), and delete the row when the customer leaves. If the team later wants the basket items, that's a new purpose, and it gets its own decision.

sections.h: The law as of November 2026, and what it asks of systems
sections.html:
This section is not legal advice. Laws differ between countries, change often, and are read differently by regulators and courts. Ask a privacy lawyer before you rely on any of it.

The GDPR has applied in the EU since 25 May 2018. Besides the principles in the last section, two parts of it turn into engineering work. Article 17 gives people the right to have their personal data erased "without undue delay", with exceptions, such as financial records a company must keep by law. Article 22 covers automated decisions, as in the Uber case.

The European Data Protection Board (EDPB), where the EU's data regulators work together, checked erasure across Europe in 2025 and published its report on 18 February 2026. 32 data protection authorities took part, and 764 companies and other organisations answered. The EDPB rated how well they follow the rules as "average". The problems it found again and again are engineering problems. There was no written erasure procedure, retention periods were hard to define, and backups weren't cleaned (raised by half of the authorities). And anonymization, stripping out whatever identifies a person, was used in place of deletion. Where backups can't be edited, organisations should keep a record of erasure requests and apply it again whenever they restore one. They should also be able to check and show that erasure happened.

Other rules start in 2026 and after. In the table, ADMT means automated decision-making technology, and a data broker is a company that buys and sells data about people. The EU AI Act is the EU's law on AI. Its annexes, lists at the end of the law, name the high-risk uses:

Rule What it asks of systems Applies from
California: rules under the CCPA, its privacy law, on risk assessments, security audits and ADMT risk assessments for risky uses of data; audits phased in over several years 1 January 2026
California: the ADMT rules for significant decisions duties for automated decisions about people 1 January 2027
California: Delete Act, the DROP platform, one place to ask every data broker to delete you registered data brokers process deletion requests from DROP at least every 45 days; $200 per request per day for failing 1 August 2026
EU AI Act, Article 50 tell people they are dealing with AI; label content an AI made (systems already on the market have until 2 December 2026 to add the marking) 2 August 2026
EU AI Act, stand-alone high-risk systems (Annex III: hiring, credit scoring and others) the high-risk duties, logging and human oversight among them 2 December 2027
EU AI Act, AI in regulated products (Annex I) the same, for products such as medical devices and machinery 2 August 2028
EU Data Act access to the data of connected products; easier switching between cloud providers, companies that rent out computers 12 September 2025; access by design for products placed on the market after 12 September 2026; switching charges abolished from 12 January 2027
India: core duties of the DPDP Act, its data protection law consent, and duties for those who hold personal data 13 May 2027

The AI Act dates are new. A later law, the Digital Omnibus on AI, in force since 27 July 2026, moved the high-risk deadlines back. Anything written in 2024 or 2025 that says August 2026 for hiring and credit systems is out of date.

Most of these rules come down to two pieces of engineering: knowing where every copy of a person's data lives, and being able to remove it. Next, we'll try that on a system built never to forget.

try.title: Match three features to the rules
steps: Picture a company that runs in the EU and in California. For each feature, name the rules from this section that apply and the date that matters. This is a sketch to bring to a lawyer, not an answer.

1. A model that automatically freezes the accounts of shops it scores as fraudulent. 2. A chatbot, a program that answers in conversation, for cardholders' questions about payments they dispute. 3. A screening model that ranks job applicants for the company's own engineering jobs.
try.expect:
1. GDPR Article 22 if the shops are run by individuals (sole traders), as in the Uber case: a fully automated freeze with significant effects needs a person who can review it, plus information about how it decides. Under the California rules, automated decision-making used for significant decisions has duties from 1 January 2027. Freezing accounts for fraud isn't one of the AI Act's high-risk uses listed in this section, but check with a lawyer.

  2. EU AI Act Article 50, since 2 August 2026: tell people they are talking to an AI. The GDPR covers the conversation data: its purpose, how long it's kept, and erasure.

  3. EU AI Act Annex III, hiring: high-risk duties from 2 December 2027, not August 2026. GDPR Article 22 if no person makes the decision. California's ADMT rules for significant decisions, such as jobs, from 1 January 2027. Mobley v. Workday shows that the seller of the model can be sued as well.

sections.h: Erasing one person from a system built never to forget
sections.html:
Almost everything in this course keeps data on purpose. Delete a row in PostgreSQL, a popular database program, and copies survive for a while. The WAL, the log of changes the database writes first, has one. Old versions of the row stay until VACUUM, its cleanup job, removes them. Replicas on other machines keep it until they replay the delete, and last night's backup has it too. Erasure has to reach every copy, and each has its own way out and its own clock:

  • Kafka, a program that keeps named logs of messages called topics, deletes old data in whole chunks, called segments, after 7 days by default. A compacted topic keeps only the newest value for each key. There a tombstone, a record with an empty value, removes older values for its own key only. The segment being written is never compacted, and max.compaction.lag.ms, the setting that would force compaction in time, defaults to never. A customer's name inside an OrderPlaced event keyed by order number is never removed by compaction at all (Partitions and segments on disk, in the Messaging and logs track).
  • An event-sourced log keeps every change as an event, so the state can be rebuilt by replaying them (the Stream processing track). It's meant to be kept for ever, and deleting events breaks the replay it exists for.
  • An LSM store writes sorted files and merges them later (the Storage engines track). A tombstone hides a value at once, but the old bytes go only when merging has reached every level.
  • In an Iceberg table, a format for big tables kept as files on cheap storage (the lakehouse of the Batch processing track), a DELETE can write a small delete file instead of rewriting the data. The old bytes stay until the data file is rewritten. Then expire_snapshots removes the old versions of the table that still point at it, and a cleanup removes files nothing points at (Row-level changes, in the Batch processing track). Until then, time travel, reading an old version of the table, still finds the deleted rows.
  • Search indexes, caches (whose entries last for a set time to live, or TTL) and ML features, the inputs prepared for machine-learning models, each need the deletion to reach them. A slow reader misses a tombstone altogether once delete.retention.ms (1 day by default) has removed it.
  • Backups need the EDPB's erasure record, applied again on every restore.

Crypto-shredding handles the copies you can't edit. Encrypt each person's personal fields with a key, the secret that locks and unlocks them, that belongs to that person alone, and keep the keys in a separate store with short backups of their own. To erase someone, delete their key. Every copy of their encrypted data, wherever it is, becomes unreadable at once, and the log still replays.

In the lab, one customer's 24 events go from 24 readable to 0, while every shop's total stays the same. Restoring the key store from an older backup brings all 24 back, unless the restore applies the erasure record again.

Is that erasure in law? Nobody has settled it. The encrypted data still exists, and this course's research found no EDPB statement accepting a deleted key as erasure. Commentary on the EDPB's 2025 guidelines on blockchains (logs shared by many parties who don't trust each other) says they treat a deleted key as making data unreadable only until the encryption can be broken. What stays readable (the customer's stand-in ID, amounts, shops, times) may still identify the person if anyone can link the stand-in ID back.

So treat crypto-shredding as a strong measure that makes erasure fast across copies, and combine it with the rest. Keep personal data, often called PII (personally identifiable information), out of events where you can: store a reference to a store you can delete from. Key the topics that do hold it by person, with compaction forced in time. Expire old table versions on a schedule. Then scan to show that the person is gone.

try.title: Erase one customer from a log that never changes
steps: From the labs folder, run the demo below. It makes 1,000 payment events by 50 customers, each with their own key. Then it erases cust-017, replays the log, and restores last night's key backup twice.
Predict the four decryptable numbers before it prints.
Which line of output would you show an auditor as proof of erasure, and what would they still ask about?

code.title: ShredDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: val backup = keys.backup() // last night's backup of the key store erase(ana, keys, ledger) // forget the key, record the request val after = rebuild(store, keys) // replay the whole log keys.restore(backup, ErasureLedger()) // a restore that knows nothing keys.restore(backup, ledger) // a restore that re-applies erasures

try.expect:
1000 events, 8 merchants; cust-017 has 24 events
plaintext emails found in the raw log: 0

before: decryptable 24 of 24, row CustomerView(name=Customer 17, email=zz-plain-17@example.com, payments=24, totalCents=241487)
after:  decryptable 0 of 24, row CustomerView(name=[erased], email=[erased], payments=24, totalCents=241487)
events still in the log: 1000; merchant totals unchanged: true

restore the backup, no ledger:   decryptable 24 of 24
restore the backup, with ledger: decryptable 0 of 24

The log never held a readable email. After the key is gone, none of the 24 events can be decrypted, while all 1,000 events and every total survive the replay. The careless restore undoes the erasure completely; the one that applies the ledger keeps it. An auditor would accept decryptable 0 of 24 as evidence. Then they would ask where else the key could be (caches, other backups, an export from the key service) and whether the customer token still links to the person anywhere.

sections.h: What to do with all of this, on the first system you work on
sections.html:
None of this needs new tools. It needs a week of looking at a system with the questions this course taught you to ask. Here are seven things to do on the first system you work on, in the order I'd do them:

  1. Draw the data map for one service, one program and the data it owns. Mark every place a customer's data is written, including topics, caches, search, the lakehouse, metrics, log lines and backups, and which copy is worked out from which. Name the system of record.
  2. For each copy, write down how a deletion reaches it and how long that takes. That list is your real erasure time. Mark every copy with no answer.
  3. Hunt for defaults that keep data for ever. Look for compacted topics with max.compaction.lag.ms untouched, Iceberg tables that never expire old versions, emails and card numbers in log lines, and backups with no erasure record.
  4. Take personal data out of events where you can, keeping a reference to a store you can delete from. Or encrypt it with a key per person, and keep the key store's backups short and separate.
  5. Add one audit from Trust, but verify: rebuild one view from its log and compare it, and check one hand-over to another system before it sends anything you can't undo.
  6. For one automated decision, such as blocking a card or holding a payout, log its inputs, model version and reasons with the request ID. Measure its error rates for the groups you're allowed to measure, and make sure a person can reach a human who can overturn it.
  7. Delete one dataset nobody uses. It's the cheapest privacy work there is.

Start with the data map. Every other item on the list needs it, and most teams find a copy they didn't know they had.

This last lesson added one thing to everything before it: the records are about people. People can be harmed by a wrong copy, a copy kept too long, or a decision nobody can explain. The tools are the ones this course built: know where every copy is, derive copies so you can rebuild them, check them, and make deleting as deliberate as writing.

try.title: Start the data map for one app
steps: Pick the payments app from this course, or an app you know well. List every place it might store a customer's personal data, directly or through something worked out from it.
For each one, write how a deletion would reach it and roughly how long that would take. Leave a question mark where you don't know.
try.expect:
A sketch for the payments app's refunds (yours will differ):

Copy How a deletion reaches it How long
refunds table in the database (system of record) DELETE by customer ID, in the erasure job at once; the database's change logs and archives as long as they are kept
refund-events topic, deleted by age time retention up to 7 days, plus the time until the segment closes
customer-profile topic, compacted a tombstone keyed by customer ID ? (max.compaction.lag.ms is at its default)
search index for the support team's tool its reader deletes by ID when it sees the tombstone seconds, if the reader is less than 1 day behind
cache in Redis, an in-memory store each entry expires on its own timer 1 hour
Iceberg table refunds_daily DELETE, then the weekly rewrite and expire_snapshots up to 12 days
nightly database backups the erasure record, applied again on restore ? (no process yet)
the app's log files ? (emails appear in two log lines) 30 days

The question marks are the work: the compacted topic needs compaction forced in time, the backups need an erasure record, and the log lines need the emails taken out. Most teams find at least one copy they didn't know about, often a log line or an export made for analysis.

opening:
Picture paying for groceries. Your card is declined. The bank's app says the payment was blocked as possible fraud, and the person on the phone says the computer decided and they can't see why. Your neighbour had the same thing last month. Across town, almost nobody does.

The program that blocked you never saw where you live or who you are. Its makers left those details out on purpose, so it felt fair to them. That's the trap: leaving a detail out feels like leaving the information out, and with data it rarely is.

In Trust, but verify, we checked that every copy says what the log says. This last lesson of the course asks harder questions. Should the copy exist at all, and who answers when a decision built from it is wrong? We'll measure unfairness in a model that never sees the group, treat personal data as a risk, read the main laws as of November 2026, and erase one customer from a log that never changes. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started this course in a café, where the owner's app showed a balance of 49.00 while the true balance was 9.00. The log of payments was right; every other number was a copy of it. Since then we've kept copies right through crashes, slow networks, split regions and silent bugs, and finally asked whether a copy should exist at all.

For the next app you build or use, ask the café's question of every number on the screen: which is the record, and which is a copy? Then ask two new ones: who does this data describe, and how would it be forgotten?

That's the end of the course. Go and build something people can trust with their records.

worked.title: Erasure time for one customer, copy by copy

steps.say: The request arrives. The erasure job deletes the customer's rows in the system of record, and writes a tombstone for their key to the compacted customer-profile topic.
steps.code:
t = 0      DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 'cust-017'
           produce("customer-profile", key = "cust-017", value = null)

steps.say: The compacted topic: the tombstone sits in the segment being written, which is never compacted. With segment.ms at its 7-day default on a quiet topic, nothing can be cleaned until that segment closes.
steps.code:
segment.ms            = 604800000             (7 days)
max.compaction.lag.ms = 9223372036854775807   (never forced)
worst case: the old value is readable for days, with no deadline

steps.say: Set both settings to the erasure deadline you promised, and the cleaner has to get there in time. The tombstone itself stays for delete.retention.ms (1 day by default), so every reader has a day to see it.
steps.code:
segment.ms            = 86400000    (1 day)
max.compaction.lag.ms = 172800000   (2 days)
delete.retention.ms   = 86400000    (1 day)

steps.say: The Iceberg table: the DELETE writes a delete file at once, but the bytes stay in the old data files. A weekly job rewrites the data files, and a daily job expires versions of the table older than 5 days.
steps.code:
day 0   DELETE FROM refunds_daily WHERE customer_id = 'cust-017'
day 7   rewrite_data_files   (new files without the rows)
day 12  expire_snapshots     (the last snapshot that points at the old files is now 5 days old)
worst case: about 12 days, plus orphan-file cleanup

steps.say: The events were crypto-shredded, so they are unreadable as soon as the key is gone. The slowest copy sets the total, so that is where to work.
steps.code:
event log (key deleted)       at once
customer-profile topic        within 2 days (after tuning)
Iceberg table                 about 12 days
backups                       on the next restore, via the erasure record

lab.title: Crypto-shred a customer from an event log that never changes
steps: From the labs folder, run the tests once. 9 tests run, and all fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's way of saying "not written yet", because setting up the store already needs encryption. Events.kt is finished: the event, the store that encrypts each event as it is added, and the made-up customers.

In Gcm.kt, write seal and open with the JDK's own javax.crypto. Use AES/GCM/NoPadding, a standard way to encrypt that also detects tampering, with a 128-bit tag (its check value) and the person's ID as associated data, which is checked but not encrypted. The first two tests check the round trip, and that a wrong key or person fails.

In Keys.kt, write forget (remove the key and overwrite its bytes with zeros) and restore. Read the test restoring last night's key backup brings the erased customer back first: it shows why restore needs the ledger.
In Projection.kt, write rebuild and decryptable. A person with no key shows as [erased]; a record that fails its tag check while its key exists must throw an error.
Run all the tests until they pass. Then look at the test with the damaged record, and explain why it must fail loudly instead of showing [erased].
hints: seal: Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding"), then init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, GCMParameterSpec(TAG_BITS, iv)), updateAAD(aad) and doFinal(plaintext). open is the same with DECRYPT_MODE.
restore: clear the map, put in a copy of each backed-up key, then call forget for every subject in erased.subjects.
rebuild: keys.lookup(e.subject) is null for an erased person. Don't wrap Gcm.open in runCatching there, which would hide the error; in decryptable you may, since it only counts.

drill.title: Erasure and accountability, from memory
drill.prompt: Without notes: (1) write the steps of a handler for an erasure request, in a system with an event log, a key store with backups, and a compacted topic; (2) list three things a system needs so that a person can contest an automated decision; (3) give the EU AI Act date for high-risk hiring and credit-scoring systems, and the date the Article 50 transparency duty started; (4) say in one sentence why the legal status of crypto-shredding is open.

answer.html:
(1) delete the person's rows in the system of record
    forget their data key, and write their ID into the erasure ledger
    produce a tombstone for their key on the compacted topic (with a bounded
    max.compaction.lag.ms and segment.ms) so every consumer deletes too
    on any restore: restore the keys, then forget everyone in the ledger
    afterwards: scan every store for the person's identifiers and record the result
(2) a record of each decision: inputs, model version, reasons, request id;
    a human review queue with the power to overturn;
    a way for the person to see why, contest it and correct the data used
(3) 2 December 2027 (Annex III, after the Digital Omnibus on AI);
    Article 50 transparency from 2 August 2026
(4) the ciphertext still exists, and no regulator has said that destroying the
    key counts as erasing the data

recap: Models learn from records of past decisions, so proxies such as postcodes carry unfairness in after the group's column is removed. COMPAS wrongly labelled 44.9% of Black and 23.5% of white defendants high risk; Optum's cost proxy picked 17.7% Black patients where need would have picked 46.5%. Measure error rates for each group, and watch for feedback loops.

A decision made by software alone needs someone to answer for it: a record of its inputs, model version and reasons, a person who can overturn it, and a way to contest it. The Dutch regulator fined Uber €824,990,000 for automated shut-outs without these (August 2026, under appeal).

Privacy is the right to decide what to reveal; consent is weaker than it looks; and personal data is a risk: 23andMe's genetic data was sold in bankruptcy for $305 million. Collect less, use it only for its purpose, and give every dataset an end date.

As of November 2026: the GDPR's erasure and automated-decision rules, the EDPB's findings on erasure in backups, California's 2026 rules and the Delete Act's DROP, the AI Act's high-risk dates moved to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028, and the Data Act. This is not legal advice.

Erasure must reach every copy: topics, compaction, LSM tombstones, Iceberg snapshots, views and backups. Crypto-shredding makes the copies you can't edit unreadable at once, and every restore must apply the erasure record again.
The limit: whether a deleted key counts as erasure in law is still open, and no technique fixes a decision that should never have been automated. Those calls belong to people, with a lawyer at hand.

explain.prompt: Someone on a product team says: "We keep everything in an event log so we can replay it. Erasure is the lawyers' problem, and anyway we delete the customer's row." Explain why erasure is an engineering problem in this design, and what you would build.
explain.answer: Deleting the customer's row erases one copy. The same person's data is in every event in the log, which we keep on purpose so we can replay it, and in everything worked out from it: the topics, the search index, the caches, the lakehouse table with its old versions, and the backups of all of them. An erasure request has to reach each copy, and each one has its own mechanism and its own deadline, so it's a dataflow problem like any other in our system. I'd start with a data map of every copy. Then I'd encrypt personal fields in events with a key per customer, so that deleting the key makes every copy of those events unreadable at once while the replay still works for totals. Topics that hold personal data would be keyed by customer, with compaction forced in time. The lakehouse would get scheduled rewrites and expiry of old versions. The key store would get its own short backups, plus an erasure ledger that every restore applies again. Afterwards a scan shows the person is gone, since the regulators ask us to show erasure. The lawyers decide what we must keep and for how long; whether we can actually erase is ours. And none of this is legal advice: a lawyer should confirm whether a deleted key is enough in our case, because that question is still open.

deeper.html:
Why fairness has no single number. In the COMPAS debate, the tool's maker answered ProPublica that its scores were equally predictive for both groups: among people given the same score, about the same share reoffended. ProPublica's numbers were about something else, the error rates among people who did not reoffend. Its errors in the other direction ran the other way: of those who did reoffend, 47.7% of white defendants had been labelled lower risk, against 28.0% of Black defendants. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2016) and Chouldechova (2017) showed that when the groups' underlying rates differ, a score generally can't meet both definitions at once. That's a property of the arithmetic, not of one model, so a team has to choose which errors it cares about, say so, and measure them.

Prices can loop too. A study of German petrol stations (Assad, Clark, Ershov and Xu, a 2020 working paper) found that in markets with two stations, margins didn't change when one station started setting prices by algorithm, and rose 28% when both did. Two programs that each learn from the other's prices can drift towards higher prices without anyone agreeing to it.

Erasure costs performance. Shastri and colleagues measured what GDPR-style features (extra data kept for each record, timely deletion, logs of who read what) do to databases such as Redis and PostgreSQL (PVLDB, 2020). Design them in early. Adding an erasure path to a system built to keep everything is far harder than keeping a customer's data in one partition or under one key from the start.

Pseudonymous isn't anonymous. The EDPB has warned against calling data anonymous when it is only pseudonymous, replaced by stand-in IDs that someone could link back. That matters for crypto-shredding: whatever stays readable after a key is deleted is still personal data if it can be linked to the person.

Fines aren't final until the courts are done. In March 2026 a Luxembourg court annulled Amazon's €746 million GDPR fine, while agreeing that the breaches happened, and sent the case back to the regulator. Uber's appeal of its fine is still open.

Where to read the law itself. The GDPR is short enough to read in an evening, and its Articles 5, 17, 22 and 25 (data protection by design and by default) are the ones engineers meet. The EDPB publishes its guidelines and its coordinated-action reports, and the CPPA, California's privacy agency, publishes California's rules in full. Read them with a lawyer, not instead of one.

The ethical framing of this lesson, data as a liability and privacy as a right to decide, follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 14; the cases, numbers and legal dates come from 2025 and 2026 sources.
